nameStory: The locust borer gets its name from its favorite food: black locust trees. These beetles are so closely tied to locust trees that they've built their entire life cycle around them, boring tunnels through the wood as larvae and feeding on the flowers as adults.
description: The locust borer is a striking longhorn beetle with bold yellow and black stripes that make it look like a wasp at first glance. These medium-sized beetles have the characteristically long antennae that give longhorn beetles their name. Adults are typically around half an inch to three-quarters of an inch long, with a robust, cylindrical body that's built for tunneling through wood.

idTips.label: Yellow and black stripes
idTips.description: Bright golden-yellow bands cross the shiny black wing covers in a distinctive pattern that mimics wasps - look for the W-shaped marking that often forms across the back

idTips.label: Long antennae
idTips.description: Antennae are nearly as long as the body, with distinct segments that feel rigid when gently touched - much longer than typical beetles

idTips.label: Robust body
idTips.description: Body feels solid and heavy for its size, with a smooth, hard shell that makes a slight clicking sound when tapped

idTips.label: Location on black locust
idTips.description: Almost always found on or near black locust trees - look for them on the fragrant white flower clusters or crawling on the deeply furrowed bark

idTips.label: Clumsy flight
idTips.description: Flies with a heavy, buzzing sound and tends to bump into things - much less graceful than the wasps they mimic

habitat: Look for locust borers wherever black locust trees grow in New England - along roadsides, forest edges, old fields, and disturbed soils. Black locusts thrive in poor, sandy, or clay soils and can tolerate urban conditions, so you'll often find these beetles in parks, vacant lots, and suburban areas. They're most common at lower elevations but can be found throughout the region where their host trees have been planted or naturalized.

seasonality.spring: Adults are just emerging and may be sluggish in cool weather. Look for exit holes in black locust bark where new adults have chewed their way out.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity time! Adults are most visible in late summer, feeding on goldenrod flowers and mating. This is when you're most likely to spot their distinctive yellow and black stripes.
seasonality.fall: Adults die off after mating, but larvae are actively tunneling inside locust trees. Listen for faint chewing sounds or look for fresh sawdust at the base of trees.
seasonality.winter: Larvae continue developing inside tree trunks, invisible but still growing. No surface activity, but you might find old exit holes in the bark.

funFact: Locust borers are master mimics that have evolved to look almost exactly like wasps, complete with yellow and black warning colors - but they're completely harmless to humans and can't sting at all, making them one of nature's most convincing bluffs!
confusionNotes: Most people mistake locust borers for wasps or yellow jackets because of their bold yellow and black stripes. The giveaway is the antennae - wasps have shorter, more curved antennae, while locust borers have the distinctively long, straight antennae of longhorn beetles. Memory trick: "Long antennae = longhorn beetle, not a wasp."
contextualKnowledge: The "locust" in both the beetle's name and its host tree is a case of mistaken identity - early American settlers called black locust trees "locusts" because their seedpods reminded them of Middle Eastern locust trees, though they're completely unrelated. True locusts are grasshoppers, not trees or beetles!
compareHints: As the only Megacyllene species in New England, locust borers are most easily confused with other longhorn beetles in the region. However, most other longhorns lack the bold wasp-like yellow and black striping pattern. The combination of bright yellow bands on black wing covers and the exclusive association with black locust trees makes locust borers fairly unique among New England's longhorn beetle family.
